response.passage: The French society before 1789 was divided into three estates, where the burden of taxation fell entirely on the Third Estate. The First and Second Estates, comprising the clergy and nobility, enjoyed feudal privileges and were exempt from paying taxes to the King. The Third Estate, which included peasants, workers, and the middle class, faced a severe subsistence crisis due to bad harvests and rising bread prices. When the Estates General met, the King insisted on the old system where each estate had only one vote, rather than giving every individual representative a vote. This injustice sparked the formation of the National Assembly. Meanwhile, the storming of the Bastille was driven by rumors of military action, even though the fortress held only seven prisoners at the time. Later, the Jacobins, a political club led by Maximilien Robespierre, emerged as a radical group representing the poorer sections of society, distinct from the wealthy aristocracy. While the Revolution promised liberty, it did not grant voting rights to women, who remained excluded from political participation. Furthermore, Napoleon Bonaparte later rose to power, but he was not a democratic leader; he established a military dictatorship that curtailed many revolutionary freedoms. The struggle for equality was long, and even the abolition of slavery was temporary, as it was reintroduced by Napoleon after being briefly ended by the Convention.
response.summary: French society was deeply unequal, with the Third Estate bearing the tax burden while the nobility enjoyed privileges. The Revolution brought political changes, but it failed to grant universal rights and eventually led to Napoleon's authoritarian rule.
